chapter: Army band, Lena Horne, Billie Holiday and the 1950s
title: Twin Falls, Idaho gig and missing The Benny Goodman Story
summary: While Lena was away Horace took a five-month job at the Turf Club in Twin Falls and Pocatello with his four-piece band, and Goodman's people could not find him to give him a part in The Benny Goodman Story.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: So she and Lennie took a little tour, and she said, 'I want you to be available when I come back.' So, she was supposed to have been gone about three months. Well, she was gone about six. Well, I begin to get restless, so I used to hang around down on Central Avenue at a place called the Club Alabam, with a great band, swingin' band down there, and you must have known this guy. A guy named Johnny Otis.
Oh yeah. He's still doing a thing today.

Johnny Otis was playing the Club Alabam, and there was a band down there called Harlan Leonard and his Kansas City Rockets. They were there in California. So I happened to have been down there one day, and just foolin'

around. So here's a guy comes in from Twin Falls, Idaho. Here's a little story for you. And he walked up to me, and he said, "I'm lookin' for a four piece band to go to play about five months in Twin Falls, Idaho. I can pay $600, room and board." I said, "Come this way, sir." And this guy -- this really happened. So I had my group I was rehearsing, because I was getting restless. I accepted that job. You know, we went to Twin Falls, Idaho, and it was a beautiful thing, and this is how I started my group, my small group, and while I was in Twin Falls, Idaho, playing this date -- I think it lasted about five months -- Lena Horne had come back to the States, and she couldn't find me. And this is one of the reasons why I didn't get the part in The Benny Goodman Story." They couldn't locate me.
They didn't know where you were.

Fletcher's wife tried to find me, and I wasn't a good writer anyway. So they took Sammy Davis, Sr. to play in The Benny Goodman Story, instead of me. They looked all over for me. Nobody knew where I was. I was in a little obsolete town, Pocatello, Idaho, you know, which you had to get a magnifying glass to find on the map. But this is what happened.
Now, when was this? Do you recall what year, or -- probably late forties?
Yeah. Well, it was a year before the picture came out, you know.

Benny Goodman tried to find me. They all tried to find me, you know. But I was happy with the group back in again, and this was a nice salary, with room and board. I had a little saxophone with me from Boston, Massachusetts named Smiley Thompson. He could play. A little bitty guy, but he was tight financially. And I got to tell you, this is real funny. And the guy that we played for was the President of the Cattle Owners' Association of the State of Idaho. And we had nothin' but steaks, you know, food. Anything we wanted at this particular club. It was called the Turf Club. Smiley, the saxophone player, picked up about 35 pounds. He couldn't get into any of his clothes. He had to buy new wardrobe.
He had to spend about $500, man, to buy everything new. His shoes got too small! No shirts would fit him. No underwear, or nothin'. It was a fun thing, you know. Boy, and we fell out. There.
This was in Twin Falls or Pocatello?
This was in Twin Falls, but he had another club in Pocatello, so we played both places. But man, that was a great experience. And then I came back down to Los Angeles, but it was too late.
